newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration still opposed to vouchers.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration still opposed to vouchers.

text.p: Education Secretary Richard Riley Tuesday repeated the Clinton administration's strong opposition to educational vouchers, saying they would sap resources from public schools at a crucial time.
Riley praised the Supreme Court's ruling Monday that public school teachers may conduct remedial classes at parochial schools and said the administration strongly supported the decision.

But in a statement issued late Tuesday, Riley said the administration remained opposed, on policy grounds, to educational vouchers that would enable parents to send their children to private schools with federal funds.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich last week again called for Congress to pass legislation allowing educational vouchers.

"While we support choice within the public school system, private school vouchers would drain much-needed resources from public schools at a time of increasing enrollments and demands on our public schoool systems," Riley said Tuesday.
Instead, he said, limited government resources should be focused on improving public schools which continued to serve the overwhelming majority of students.
"Private school vouchers would also make parochial schools less parochial and private schools less private -- subjecting them to public supervision and compromising their independence," Riley said.

In Monday's decision, the high court overturned its own 12-year-old ruling in an important church-state case and ruled that allowing public school teachers into private schools for remedial classes does not violate the constitutional requirement of separation of church and state.

The decision was a victory for the Clinton administration, which argued that the 1985 Supreme Court ruling made it more difficult and costly to provide remedial educational and counselling services to low-income students in private schools.
